title: How do we find a corner that is four centimetres from both ends?
description: A base of four centimetres is drawn, and an arc of the same opening is swung from each end. The crossing of the arcs is the third corner, and the board shows why both new sides are four centimetres. Keeko doubts the arcs and wants to mark the corner by eye.
teaching_notes: One idea: every place on an arc is the same distance from its centre, so the crossing of two arcs of the same opening is the same distance from both ends. Watch for children who place the third corner by eye with a ruler and stop when the sides look equal.

source: Construct a triangle in which all the sides are of length 4
video_script.why: The child has met the idea of a circle as all the places at one distance from a centre and now uses it to place the third corner of a triangle with equal sides.
video_script.substitution: The base is four centimetres and each arc has a four centimetre opening, so the crossing is four centimetres from both ends.
video_script.anchor: A base of four centimetres with two arcs of four centimetres crossing above it
video_script.wrong_answer: mark the third corner by eye
video_script.wrong_move: A child marks the third corner by eye with a ruler and stops when the two new sides look equal, though a corner that looks right can be a little out.
video_script.payoff_line: The triangle is equilateral, with every side four centimetres long.

final_answer.spoken: an equilateral triangle with all sides four centimetres

never_show: the word equilateral before the answer beat
maths_rules: arc from A with radius 4 cm: every place on it is 4 cm from A
arc from B with radius 4 cm: every place on it is 4 cm from B
C is on both arcs, so AC = 4 cm and BC = 4 cm
AB = BC = CA = 4 cm, so the triangle is equilateral
video_script.design: One idea: the crossing of two arcs of the same opening is the same distance from both ends. One base, two arcs in two colours, and the third corner where they cross; Keeko's doubt closes the video.
